chunks.section_title: Section 41B — Compulsory disclosure of information by the occupier
chunks.text:
Section 41B — Compulsory disclosure of information by the occupier

The occupier of a factory involving a hazardous process must disclose
all information concerning the dangers of that process, including
health hazards and the measures to overcome them, to the workers
employed in the factory, to the Chief Inspector, to the local
authority, and to the general public in the vicinity.

The duty runs to the workers directly, not only to the regulator. A
hazard assessment that exists in a file submitted to an authority, and
that the people working alongside the substance have never been shown,
does not discharge this obligation.

At the time of registering a factory involving a hazardous process, the
occupier must lay down a detailed policy with respect to the health and
safety of the workers, and must communicate it to the Chief Inspector
and the local authority.

The occupier must draw up an on-site emergency plan and detailed
disaster control measures, and must make known to the workers employed
and to the general public living in the vicinity the safety measures
required to be taken in the event of an accident. A plan that has not
been communicated to the people who would have to act on it is not an
emergency plan; it is a document about one.

Workers must be informed of the imminent danger to their health and
safety arising from any accident or from any process, and of the
remedial action to be taken.

chunks.section_title: Section 41C — Specific responsibility in relation to hazardous processes
chunks.text:
Section 41C — Specific responsibility in relation to hazardous processes

The occupier of every factory involving a hazardous process must
maintain accurate and up-to-date health records, or medical records, of
the workers who are exposed to any chemical, toxic or other harmful
substance which is manufactured, stored, handled or transported in the
factory. Those records must be accessible to the workers subject to
prescribed conditions.

The occupier must appoint persons who possess the qualifications and
experience prescribed for handling the hazardous substances involved,
and who are competent to supervise that handling. Supervision of a
hazardous process by a person qualified only in general production
management does not satisfy this requirement.

The occupier must provide for medical examination of every worker
before their employment in a hazardous process, and thereafter at
intervals not exceeding those prescribed, for as long as the worker
continues to be employed in that process. Where a worker is found to
have contracted an occupational disease, they must not be employed in
that process until they have been certified fit.

chunks.section_title: Section 41H — Right of workers to warn about imminent danger
chunks.text:
Section 41H — Right of workers to warn about imminent danger

Where workers employed in a factory carrying on a hazardous process
have reasonable apprehension that there is a likelihood of imminent
danger to their lives or health, they may bring the matter to the
notice of the occupier, the agent, the manager or any other person in
charge of the factory, directly or through their representatives.

The person so notified must take immediate remedial action if satisfied
that there is a likelihood of imminent danger, and must send a report
of the action taken to the nearest Inspector.

If the person notified is not satisfied that there is such a
likelihood, they must refer the matter to the nearest Inspector
immediately, and the Inspector's decision on the question is final.

The practical significance of this section is that it places the duty
to act on the recipient of the warning, on a timescale set by the
danger rather than by the convenience of production. A worker who
reports a smell of gas, a leaking valve or an unlabelled drum has
discharged their part; the obligation then sits with the person in
charge, and deferring the question to a later shift or a scheduled
meeting is not compliance.

Section 87 — Dangerous operations

Where the State Government is satisfied that any operation carried on
in a factory exposes the persons employed in it to a serious risk of
bodily injury, poisoning or disease, it may make rules applicable to
that operation.

Such rules may prohibit or restrict the employment of women,
adolescents or children in that operation; require periodical medical
examination of the persons employed and prohibit the employment of any
person not certified fit; require the provision of protective
equipment, of washing facilities and of accommodation for clothing kept
off during the operation; and require the exhaust of fumes, dust and
other impurities at their point of origin rather than their dilution in
the general workroom air.

The preference for control at source over general ventilation is
deliberate. Diluting a contaminant across a workroom reduces the
measured concentration without removing the exposure, and it moves the
hazard to workers who have no involvement in the operation that
produced it.

chunks.section_title: Section 38 — Precautions in case of fire
chunks.text:
Section 38 — Precautions in case of fire

Every factory must be provided with such means of escape in case of
fire as may be prescribed, and the means of escape must be maintained
free of obstruction and available for use at all material times.

Every factory must be provided with effective and clearly audible means
of giving warning in the case of fire to every person employed in it. A
warning system that is inaudible over the noise of the plant it
protects does not satisfy this requirement.

Every door affording a means of escape must not be locked or fastened
so that it cannot be easily and immediately opened from the inside
while any person is within the factory, and every such door must, save
in prescribed cases, be constructed to open outwards. Doors locked
against theft during a shift, and doors obstructed by stored material,
are the two most common ways in which a compliant escape route becomes
a non-compliant one without anything being formally changed.

Effective measures must be taken to ensure that all the workers are
familiar with the means of escape and have been adequately trained in
the routine to be followed in the case of fire.

1910.151(c) — Emergency eyewash and drench facilities

Where the eyes or body of any person may be exposed to injurious
corrosive materials during their work, suitable facilities for quick
drenching or flushing of the eyes and body must be provided within the
work area for immediate emergency use.

The accepted interpretation of "within the work area" is that the
facility is reachable in about ten seconds of unimpeded travel, which
is commonly implemented as a distance of roughly fifteen metres on the
same level, along a path with no doors to open, no stairs to climb and
no obstruction to step around. The reason for the time limit rather
than a pure distance limit is that a casualty with a corrosive
substance in their eyes cannot see where they are going, so a route
that is short on a drawing may be impassable in practice.

Facilities must deliver clean water at a rate and for a duration
sufficient to support the irrigation times specified for the substances
in use, which for strong alkalis may be an hour or more. A unit that
delivers a brief trickle does not satisfy this requirement, and a
trickle applied to concentrated corrosives can be actively harmful.

Plumbed units should be activated weekly to flush the line and to
confirm they still function; self-contained units require their fluid
to be maintained and replaced. An eyewash that has never been tested
is, in practice, unlikely to work on the day it is needed.

1910.1200 — Hazard communication

Employers must maintain a safety data sheet for every hazardous
chemical in the workplace, and those sheets must be readily accessible
to employees in their work area during each work shift.

"Readily accessible" means the worker can get to the information
without asking permission, without a password they do not have, and
without waiting for a supervisor to unlock an office. A binder locked
in a manager's room during the night shift does not satisfy this
requirement, and neither does an electronic system that is unavailable
when the site network is down. Where sheets are held electronically, a
reliable backup must exist for the situation in which the electronic
system cannot be reached — which includes the emergency the sheets are
needed for.

Containers must be labelled with the product identifier and the
appropriate hazard warnings, and labels must not be removed or
defaced. Decanted material in an unlabelled secondary container is a
recurring cause of a responder treating the wrong substance.

Employees must be trained on the hazards of the chemicals in their work
area, on the measures they can take to protect themselves, and on the
details of the employer's hazard communication programme, at the time
of their initial assignment and whenever a new hazard is introduced.

1910.134 — Respiratory protection in IDLH atmospheres

An atmosphere that is immediately dangerous to life or health requires
a full-facepiece pressure-demand self-contained breathing apparatus, or
a combination supplied-air respirator with an auxiliary self-contained
supply. Air-purifying respirators — cartridge and canister masks — are
not adequate in an IDLH atmosphere and must not be used in one. A
cartridge mask offers no protection where the atmosphere is
oxygen-deficient, and its cartridge has a finite and unmonitored
capacity for the contaminant.

Where employees enter an IDLH atmosphere, at least one trained employee
must be located outside it, in visual, voice or signal-line
communication with those inside, equipped for and trained in rescue,
and provided with the equipment needed to effect it. The employer must
be notified before the standby person enters to attempt a rescue.

Respirators must be selected for the specific contaminant, fit-tested
to the individual wearer, inspected before each use and maintained.
Facial hair that interferes with the sealing surface prevents an
adequate seal, and a respirator that does not seal provides confidence
without protection.

1910.146 — Permit-required confined spaces

A confined space that contains or may contain a hazardous atmosphere is
a permit-required confined space, and entry to it requires a written
permit, atmospheric testing before and during entry, an attendant
stationed outside for the duration, and rescue provisions arranged
before entry rather than improvised afterwards.

Atmospheric testing must be carried out in the order oxygen first, then
flammable gases and vapours, then toxic contaminants, and must sample
the space at the top, middle and bottom. Testing only at the opening
misses exactly the stratified accumulation that makes these spaces
lethal — a heavier-than-air contaminant sits at the bottom, which is
where the worker's head will be when they reach the floor.

The attendant must remain outside the space, must monitor the
authorised entrants, and must not enter the space to attempt a rescue.
A very large proportion of confined space fatalities are would-be
rescuers who entered without equipment to help a colleague who had
collapsed, and who then collapsed for the same reason. Rescue must be
performed from outside the space wherever possible, using retrieval
equipment, and otherwise only by trained rescuers with breathing
apparatus.

chunks.section_title: 1910.120(q) — Emergency response to hazardous substance releases
chunks.text:
1910.120(q) — Emergency response to hazardous substance releases

An employer whose employees may respond to a release of a hazardous
substance must have a written emergency response plan in place before
the response, covering roles, lines of authority, communication,
evacuation routes, decontamination, and the criteria for calling in
outside assistance.

Responders must be trained to a level appropriate to the role they will
actually perform. First responders at the awareness level are trained
to recognise a release, initiate the emergency response sequence and
protect themselves — and specifically to take no further action.
Employees who will attempt to stop a release from a safe distance, or
who will approach it, require substantially more training and are
required to work under an incident command system.

No employee who has not been trained to the required level may attempt
to stop a release, plug a leak, or enter the area of a release. The
untrained employee's correct action is to raise the alarm, evacuate,
and account for people — and the plan must make this explicit, because
in the absence of an explicit instruction the instinct of a competent
worker who knows the plant is to go and deal with it.

An incident commander must be identified and must be the person who
authorises entry, sets the isolation distances and authorises re-entry
once the release is controlled.

Section 2 — Hazards Identification

Anhydrous ammonia is a colourless gas with an extremely sharp,
suffocating odour, handled industrially as a liquefied gas under
pressure and used widely as a refrigerant. It is corrosive and acutely
toxic by inhalation, and it is flammable within a narrow range.

The gas has a strong affinity for water and therefore attacks moist
tissue preferentially: eyes, mouth, throat, upper airway and any sweaty
or damp skin. Injury is alkaline in character, which matters
clinically, because alkali burns keep penetrating deeper into tissue
long after the initial contact rather than forming a limiting layer of
coagulated protein the way acid burns tend to.

Liquid ammonia released from a pressurised system flashes to gas and
absorbs a great deal of heat doing so, so direct contact with the
liquid or with the cold vapour stream produces frostbite in addition to
chemical burns. Anyone handling a liquid release is facing two
different injury mechanisms on the same square centimetre of skin.

Pure ammonia gas is lighter than air and will rise and disperse. This
is widely and dangerously over-generalised. A large release of
refrigerated liquid produces a cold, dense aerosol of gas and suspended
droplets that behaves as a heavy cloud at first, hugging the ground and
flowing into low areas exactly as chlorine would, until it warms enough
to lift. Do not treat low ground as safe during a large or refrigerated
release.

The odour is unmistakable and detectable far below harmful
concentrations, but as with chlorine it must never be used to declare
an area clear. Exposure limit is taken here as 25 ppm as an eight-hour
time-weighted average, with an IDLH value of 300 ppm. Ammonia is
flammable in air between roughly 15 and 28 per cent by volume, a range
that is hard to reach outdoors but readily reached inside a plant room.

Section 4 — First-Aid Measures

Move the affected person to fresh air, upwind of the release, and do
not attempt entry into a plant room or confined space without breathing
apparatus and a standby person.

For eye contact, irrigate immediately with clean water for at least
20 minutes, holding the eyelids open, and continue irrigation during
transport to medical care. Alkali eye injury is a genuine emergency and
the duration of irrigation is the single factor most strongly
associated with the outcome. Do not stop early because the casualty
says the pain has eased.

For skin contact, remove contaminated clothing while flushing with
copious water and continue for at least 20 minutes. Where clothing has
frozen to the skin, thaw it in place with lukewarm water rather than
pulling it away, which removes skin with it.

Do not attempt to neutralise ammonia on skin or in the eye with any
acidic solution, including vinegar, dilute acetic acid, citrus juice or
any proprietary neutraliser. Neutralisation is an exothermic reaction
occurring on already-damaged tissue and adds a thermal burn to a
chemical one. Water, in quantity, for a long time, is the treatment.

If ammonia has been swallowed, do not induce vomiting: the caustic
liquid injures the oesophagus a second time on the way back up, and
vomit may be aspirated. Do not attempt to neutralise it in the stomach.
If the casualty is fully conscious and able to swallow, small sips of
water are acceptable. Give nothing by mouth to a casualty who is
drowsy, convulsing or unconscious.

Casualties with significant inhalation exposure require medical
observation for delayed airway swelling and pulmonary oedema even if
they appear to recover at the scene.

Section 5 — Fire-Fighting Measures

Ammonia is flammable between approximately 15 and 28 per cent in air.
Outdoors it usually disperses below that range; inside a compressor
house, cold store or other enclosed plant space it can readily form an
explosive atmosphere, and that space may also contain the ignition
source.

Stop the flow of gas if the isolation valve can be reached safely. Do
not extinguish a burning ammonia release while gas continues to flow —
extinguishing the flame converts a visible, localised, largely
consumed release into an invisible toxic cloud accumulating in the same
building. Control the fire, cool the surroundings, and isolate the
source.

Use water spray to knock down and disperse vapour and to cool exposed
containers. Do not direct a water jet into a pool of liquid ammonia.
Water is much warmer than the boiling liquid and adds heat to it,
producing vigorous boiling and a far larger vapour cloud than the pool
was generating on its own. Apply water as a fine spray to the vapour
above the pool, not into the pool itself.

Water used for vapour suppression becomes strongly alkaline ammonia
solution and must be contained and prevented from entering drains or
watercourses, where it is severely toxic to fish.

Fire-fighters require self-contained breathing apparatus and full
chemical protective clothing.

Section 6 — Accidental Release Measures

Raise the alarm, evacuate crosswind then upwind, and account for
personnel by name. Ventilate enclosed plant rooms remotely if fixed
ventilation can be started from outside; do not enter to open a door or
start a fan.

Isolate the area for at least 100 metres for a small leak and
considerably further downwind for a large one. During a large or
refrigerated release, evacuate low-lying ground as well, for the reason
given in Section 2 — the initial cold cloud is dense and does not
behave like the buoyant gas that ammonia becomes later.

Only trained responders in self-contained breathing apparatus and
protective clothing may approach. Isolate at source where the valve is
reachable without entering the cloud.

Ammonia must never be mixed with chlorine, with hypochlorite bleach or
with any other chlorine donor as part of a response. The reaction
produces chloramines and potentially nitrogen trichloride, adding an
explosive and a second toxic gas to an incident that already has one.
On a site holding both substances this is the most consequential
mistake available to a responder, and it is usually made with good
intentions by someone trying to neutralise a spill.

Do not allow ammonia or ammonia-contaminated water to enter drains,
sewers or watercourses.

Section 7 — Handling and Storage

Store in a cool, dry, well-ventilated area away from heat and direct
sunlight, with cylinders upright and secured. Refrigeration plant must
have gas detection in the plant room, ventilation that can be started
from outside it, and an emergency stop that isolates the compressors
from a safe position.

Segregate ammonia from chlorine, from hypochlorites, from strong acids
and from halogens by distance or by a fire-resistant barrier. Storing
ammonia and chlorine in the same room is a recognised precursor to a
multi-substance incident and must not be done regardless of how the
containers are labelled.

Use steel or approved alloys for ammonia service. Copper, brass, bronze
and zinc and their alloys are attacked rapidly by ammonia and must
never be used for fittings, gauges, valves or lines. A brass fitting
installed as a convenient substitute is a common root cause of
subsequent releases.

Keep an eyewash station and emergency shower immediately adjacent to
any area where ammonia is transferred or decanted, and verify by test
that they run clean water at an adequate rate.

Section 10 — Stability and Reactivity

Stable under the storage conditions described above.

Reacts violently with chlorine and with hypochlorites to form
chloramines and, under some conditions, the shock-sensitive explosive
nitrogen trichloride.

Reacts vigorously and exothermically with strong acids. Neutralisation
of a bulk ammonia spill with acid is not an approved response and has
caused injury through violent boiling and spattering.

Attacks copper, brass, bronze, zinc and their alloys, and forms
explosive compounds with mercury, silver and gold salts. Mercury
manometers must not be used on ammonia systems.

Hazardous decomposition products include nitrogen oxides and, in
contact with chlorine donors, chloramines and nitrogen trichloride.

Section 2 — Hazards Identification

Sodium hydroxide, commonly called caustic soda or lye, is supplied as
white deliquescent pellets, flakes or beads, or as a colourless
solution of varying strength. It is odourless and severely corrosive to
skin, eyes and the respiratory and digestive tracts.

Alkali burns are more dangerous than acid burns of comparable strength
and are consistently underestimated at the scene, for two reasons that
matter operationally. First, alkali saponifies fat and dissolves
protein rather than coagulating it, so there is no barrier layer formed
and the injury continues to penetrate for as long as the substance
remains in contact. Second, the initial contact is often not
particularly painful — caustic solution feels soapy and slippery on the
skin, and that slipperiness is the surface layer of the worker's own
skin being dissolved. A casualty may not report a splash until
significant damage has been done.

Eye contact is a sight-threatening emergency. Alkali penetrates the
cornea within seconds and can reach the anterior chamber, and the
outcome depends heavily on how quickly and how long irrigation is
carried out.

Dissolving solid caustic soda in water releases a large amount of heat.
A concentrated solution can approach boiling in an open vessel, and hot
caustic solution splashed onto skin delivers a thermal and a chemical
burn together.

Dust from pellets or flakes is corrosive to the airway. Occupational
exposure limit is taken here as 2 mg/m³ as a ceiling value, not a
time-weighted average — the limit is not to be exceeded at any moment.

Section 4 — First-Aid Measures

For eye contact, irrigate immediately with clean water and continue for
at least 60 minutes, holding the eyelids apart, and continue during
transport to medical care. The irrigation time for alkali eye injury is
substantially longer than for acid, and stopping early because the
casualty reports relief is a recognised cause of avoidable sight loss.
Obtain ophthalmic assessment for any caustic eye exposure, however
minor it appears.

For skin contact, flush with large quantities of running water for at
least 30 minutes while removing contaminated clothing, footwear and
jewellery. Continue flushing until the slippery, soapy feel of the skin
has gone; while it persists, alkali is still present and still
reacting.

Where solid caustic pellets or flakes are on the skin, brush off the
dry material first, then irrigate with a large and continuous flow.
Wetting solid caustic with a small quantity of water generates heat and
produces a concentrated hot solution in contact with the skin, which is
worse than either the dry solid or a proper flood of water.

Do not attempt to neutralise caustic on skin or in the eye with vinegar,
citric acid, boric acid or any other acidic solution. The reaction is
exothermic and takes place on tissue that is already injured. Water, in
quantity, for a long time, is the treatment.

If swallowed, do not induce vomiting. Returning caustic across the
oesophagus a second time compounds the injury and risks aspiration into
the lungs. Do not attempt neutralisation in the stomach. Do not give
anything by mouth to a casualty who is drowsy, convulsing or
unconscious. If the casualty is fully conscious and able to swallow,
small sips of water or milk to dilute are acceptable. Obtain immediate
medical attention.

Casualties with airway exposure to dust or mist require observation for
delayed swelling.

Section 5 — Fire-Fighting Measures

Sodium hydroxide does not burn and will not support combustion. The
hazards in a fire are the heat generated when water contacts the solid,
the corrosive nature of the resulting solution, and the hydrogen
produced by caustic attacking certain metals.

Use an extinguishing medium appropriate to the surrounding fire. Where
solid caustic soda is stored, prefer dry chemical or carbon dioxide in
the immediate vicinity.

Do not apply a water jet directly onto bulk solid caustic soda. The
heat of solution is substantial, and hosing a drum of pellets produces
a hot, concentrated, strongly corrosive liquid that spreads across the
floor and spatters. Where water must be used on a surrounding fire,
apply it so that run-off does not reach stored solid caustic.

Caustic soda in contact with aluminium, zinc, tin and their alloys
liberates hydrogen, which is flammable and easily ignited. A caustic
spill onto aluminium plant or an aluminium bund inside a burning
building adds an explosion hazard.

Fire-fighters require self-contained breathing apparatus and full
chemical protective clothing. Run-off water will be strongly alkaline
and must be contained.

Section 6 — Accidental Release Measures

Evacuate the immediate area and isolate it. Responders require
alkali-resistant suit, gloves, boots and full face protection, with
respiratory protection where dust or mist is present.

For a solid spill, sweep or shovel the dry material into a labelled
container for disposal, avoiding dust generation. Do not wash a bulk
solid spill down with water as the first action; dissolving it releases
heat and converts a contained, sweepable solid into a spreading
corrosive liquid that will run into drains and low areas. Recover the
bulk dry, then wash the residue.

For a solution spill, contain with dry inert absorbent — sand, earth or
a proprietary absorbent — and prevent entry to drains, sewers and
watercourses.

Neutralisation of a contained spill with a dilute weak acid may be
carried out by trained personnel, cautiously and from the edge inward,
adding the acid slowly to the caustic. The reaction is exothermic and
adding acid quickly produces violent boiling and spattering of caustic
solution. Do not attempt to neutralise a large spill; contain it and
arrange professional removal.

Wash the area down only after the bulk material has been recovered, and
check the pH of the washings before allowing them to drain.

Section 7 — Handling and Storage

Always add caustic soda to water, slowly, with stirring, and never add
water to solid caustic soda. Water poured onto pellets generates intense
localised heat, can boil, and ejects concentrated hot caustic out of the
vessel. This ordering is the most important handling rule for this
substance, and it is the mirror image of the rule for sulphuric acid —
in both cases the concentrated material goes into the water, never the
reverse.

Keep containers tightly closed. Solid caustic soda is deliquescent: it
absorbs moisture and carbon dioxide from the air, cakes, and can
generate heat inside a drum left open in humid conditions.

Store in a cool, dry, well-ventilated area with an alkali-resistant
bunded floor that does not drain to a public sewer. Keep clear of any
area subject to flooding or roof leaks, since water reaching stored
solid caustic is itself the incident.

Segregate from acids, from water-reactive materials, and from
aluminium, zinc, tin and their alloys. Do not use aluminium containers,
funnels, scoops or fittings for caustic soda in any circumstances.

Provide an emergency shower and eyewash immediately adjacent to any
point where caustic is handled or decanted, and verify by test that
they deliver a large and sustained flow of clean water.

Section 10 — Stability and Reactivity

Stable under the storage conditions described above. Deliquescent, and
absorbs carbon dioxide from the air to form sodium carbonate.

Dissolution in water is strongly exothermic.

Reacts violently and exothermically with acids. Neutralisation of bulk
material without control of the addition rate produces boiling and
spattering.

Attacks aluminium, zinc, tin and their alloys, liberating hydrogen,
which is flammable over a very wide range in air. This reaction is the
most commonly overlooked hazard of the substance, because caustic soda
is not itself flammable and the hydrogen is generated quietly at
ordinary temperatures.

Reacts with some organic halogen compounds and with nitro compounds,
in some cases violently. Attacks glass slowly, and attacks leather,
wool and other protein materials, including the protein of skin.

Hazardous decomposition products include hydrogen on contact with
susceptible metals.

Section 2 — Hazards Identification

Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas with a sharp, penetrating odour,
shipped and stored as a liquefied gas under pressure. It is acutely
toxic by inhalation and corrosive to the eyes and the entire
respiratory tract. Exposure at low concentrations causes stinging eyes,
throat irritation and coughing; at higher concentrations it causes
chest tightness, chemical bronchitis and pulmonary oedema, which may be
fatal.

The gas is roughly two and a half times heavier than air. A release
does not disperse upward; it flows downhill and collects in pits,
trenches, sumps, basements, inspection chambers and any other low-lying
space. Personnel standing at ground level in a depression can be in a
lethal concentration while the air two metres above them is breathable.
This single property governs almost every response instruction in this
document.

The odour is detectable well below the concentration that causes
injury, which is genuinely protective, but olfactory fatigue sets in
quickly. A worker who reports that the smell has faded has very
probably not moved into cleaner air; they have lost the ability to
smell the contaminant they are still standing in. Smell must never be
used to decide that an area has become safe.

Chlorine is not itself flammable, but it is a strong oxidiser and will
vigorously support the combustion of materials that do not normally
burn readily in air. Occupational exposure limit is taken here as
0.5 ppm as an eight-hour time-weighted average, with an IDLH value of
10 ppm.

Section 4 — First-Aid Measures

Move the affected person to fresh air immediately, travelling
crosswind and then upwind of the release. Because the gas pools at low
level, moving the casualty upward and outward matters as much as moving
them away — carrying someone along a trench to a distant exit can keep
them in the cloud for the whole journey.

Do not enter a suspected chlorine atmosphere to perform a rescue
without self-contained breathing apparatus and a second trained person
standing by. Untrained rescuers entering low-lying spaces are a
recurring cause of multiple casualties from a single-casualty
incident.

If breathing has stopped, a trained responder should give assisted
ventilation using a bag-valve mask with supplemental oxygen. Direct
mouth-to-mouth ventilation is contraindicated: the rescuer inhales
contaminated air from the casualty's airway.

For eye contact, flush with clean water for at least 15 minutes,
holding the eyelids apart. For skin contact, remove contaminated
clothing while flushing and continue flushing the skin for at least
15 minutes. Contact lenses should be removed if this can be done
without delaying irrigation.

Every person with a significant inhalation exposure must be kept under
medical observation even if they appear to have recovered completely.
Pulmonary oedema can be delayed by up to 24 to 48 hours, and a casualty
who feels well at the scene may deteriorate severely overnight. Do not
discharge an exposed worker back to the floor on the strength of them
saying they feel fine.

Section 5 — Fire-Fighting Measures

Chlorine does not burn. In a fire involving chlorine containers, the
hazard is the container itself: heat raises the internal pressure and
can rupture the cylinder or actuate its fusible plug, converting a
contained inventory into a sudden large release.

Cool containers exposed to fire with water spray applied from a
protected position or an unmanned monitor, from as far away as the
equipment allows.

Do not apply water directly to a chlorine leak. Water and chlorine form
hydrochloric and hypochlorous acids, which aggressively attack the
steel of the cylinder, valve and fittings. A water jet aimed at a small
leak with the intention of knocking down the gas reliably enlarges the
leak it was aimed at, and can turn a weeping valve into an open one.
Water spray may be used at a distance to suppress and direct a vapour
cloud, but never played onto the leaking vessel or its valve.

Never immerse a leaking cylinder in water, and never place it in a tank
or drum of water or caustic solution. The internal pressure of the
cylinder is higher than the head of liquid, so the leak does not stop;
water is instead drawn into the cylinder as it empties and cools,
producing violent internal corrosion.

Fire-fighters must wear self-contained breathing apparatus and full
protective clothing. Ordinary structural fire kit does not protect
against chlorine.

Section 6 — Accidental Release Measures

Raise the alarm and evacuate immediately, moving crosswind first and
then upwind. Account for personnel by name; a headcount alone will not
identify who is still in a pit.

Establish an initial isolation zone of at least 100 metres in all
directions for a small leak, extended substantially downwind for a
large one, and deny entry to everyone without breathing apparatus.
Evacuate all low-lying areas within and beyond that radius, including
basements, cable trenches, drainage chambers and any adjacent building
with below-grade space, because the gas will find them.

Only personnel trained in chlorine emergency response, wearing
self-contained breathing apparatus and chemically resistant protective
clothing, may approach to attempt isolation. Shut off the supply at
source if the valve can be reached safely; do not attempt a repair on a
pressurised system.

If a cylinder is leaking, position it so that the leak is in the vapour
space rather than the liquid space — rotating a horizontal cylinder so
the leak points upward reduces the discharge rate by a large factor,
because liquid chlorine expands to several hundred times its volume as
gas.

Prevent the release from entering drains, sewers and watercourses.
Ventilate the area only after the source has been isolated, and
re-entry must be authorised on the basis of instrument readings, never
on the basis of smell.

Section 7 — Handling and Storage

Store cylinders upright and secured against falling, in a cool, dry,
well-ventilated area that is not below ground level and does not drain
into an occupied space. Keep the storage temperature below 45 °C and
protect containers from direct sunlight and from any radiant heat
source.

Valve protection caps must be in place whenever a cylinder is not
connected and in use. Move cylinders with a proper trolley; never lift
one by its valve or cap, and never roll or drag a cylinder to move it
across a site.

Segregate chlorine from incompatible materials by distance or by a
fire-resistant barrier, not merely by labelling. Ammonia in particular
must never be stored in the same room, and the two must never be
handled in a way that allows an accidental connection between them.
Also segregate from hydrogen, hydrocarbons, turpentine, ether, finely
divided metals and all flammable materials.

Use only equipment, gaskets and lubricants specified for chlorine
service. Ordinary oils and greases react with chlorine and have caused
ignition inside valves. Systems must be scrupulously dry, because dry
chlorine is relatively compatible with steel while wet chlorine is
severely corrosive to it.

Fixed gas detection should be installed at low level, where the gas
will actually be, rather than at head height where a detector will
report clean air during a serious release.

Section 10 — Stability and Reactivity

Chlorine is stable under the storage conditions described above. It is
a powerful oxidiser and reacts with a very wide range of materials.

Reaction with ammonia is the single most important incompatibility on a
site that holds both. Chlorine and ammonia react to form chloramines
and, under some conditions, nitrogen trichloride, which is a
shock-sensitive explosive. The reaction also generates a toxic vapour
that injures responders who arrived to deal with what they believed was
a single-substance leak. Never attempt to neutralise a chlorine release
with ammonia, or an ammonia release with chlorine or with any
hypochlorite bleach.

Mixtures of chlorine and hydrogen are explosive over a wide composition
range and can be initiated by ordinary daylight.

Chlorine reacts violently with finely divided metals, with many
organic compounds, and with turpentine and similar solvents, in several
cases igniting them without any external ignition source. Wet chlorine
corrodes most common metals. Contact with water forms hydrochloric and
hypochlorous acids.

Hazardous decomposition and reaction products include hydrogen
chloride, chloramines and nitrogen trichloride.

Section 2 — Hazards Identification

Concentrated sulphuric acid is a colourless to dark brown oily liquid,
odourless, very dense, and severely corrosive to every tissue it
contacts. It causes deep chemical burns to skin and permanent damage to
eyes, and ingestion causes severe injury to the mouth, throat,
oesophagus and stomach.

Three separate mechanisms cause injury and they are frequently confused
with one another. The acid is corrosive, so it destroys tissue
chemically. It is strongly dehydrating, so it strips water out of
organic material, which is why contact with skin, wood or paper chars
them. And it releases a large amount of heat when it mixes with water,
so a dilution that is done in the wrong order produces a thermal injury
on top of the chemical one.

Mist or vapour from hot acid, or generated by splashing, is corrosive
to the respiratory tract and eyes and is a recognised carcinogen in
occupational settings. Exposure limit is taken here as 0.2 mg/m³ as an
eight-hour time-weighted average for the mist.

The liquid is roughly 1.8 times as dense as water. A spill spreads
further and carries more mass than an equivalent visible volume of
water would suggest, and it will find floor drains readily.

Sulphuric acid is not flammable, but it generates hydrogen — which is
flammable over an extremely wide range in air and needs almost no
ignition energy — when it contacts most common metals. A contained
acid spill in a plant room can therefore become an explosion hazard
without anything having burned.

Section 4 — First-Aid Measures

Speed matters more than anything else that follows. The interval before
irrigation begins governs the depth of the eventual burn.

For skin contact, immediately flush the affected area with large
quantities of running water for at least 30 minutes, removing
contaminated clothing, footwear and watch straps while flushing.
Contaminated clothing holds acid against the skin and continues to
injure it after the visible splash has been washed away.

For eye contact, irrigate with clean water for at least 30 minutes
holding the eyelids apart, and continue irrigating during transport to
medical care.

Do not attempt to neutralise acid on skin or in the eye with sodium
bicarbonate, soap solution, lime or any other alkali. Neutralisation is
strongly exothermic, and performing it on tissue that is already burned
adds a thermal burn to a chemical one. Water in quantity, for a long
time, is the treatment.

Where dry or highly concentrated acid is present as a crust or residue,
brushing off the bulk material before irrigation is appropriate,
because the first small volume of water contacting concentrated acid
generates significant heat. Once irrigation starts, it must be with a
large and continuous flow — a trickle is worse than none, because it
supplies enough water to react and not enough to carry the heat away.

If acid has been swallowed, do not induce vomiting, which returns the
acid across the oesophagus a second time and risks aspiration. Do not
attempt neutralisation in the stomach. Do not give anything by mouth to
a casualty who is drowsy or unconscious. If the casualty is fully
conscious, small sips of water to dilute are acceptable. Obtain
immediate medical attention.

For inhalation of mist, move to fresh air and obtain medical attention;
delayed respiratory effects are possible.

Section 5 — Fire-Fighting Measures

Sulphuric acid does not burn. The hazards in a fire are the hydrogen
generated by acid attacking metal, the corrosive mist driven off by
heat, and the violent reaction of the acid with any water applied to
it.

Use dry chemical, carbon dioxide or foam appropriate to the surrounding
materials to fight a fire near an acid spill. Do not direct a water jet
onto spilled concentrated acid. The heat of mixing flashes the water to
steam at the point of contact and ejects a spray of concentrated acid
outward, over a considerably wider area than the original spill and
generally in the direction of whoever is holding the hose.

Water spray may be used to cool intact containers exposed to fire and
to knock down acid mist, provided it is not played into the liquid
itself. Water used in this way becomes acidic and must be contained.

Fire-fighters must wear self-contained breathing apparatus and full
acid-resistant protective clothing. Structural fire kit is permeable to
acid and is not adequate for a spill response.

Section 6 — Accidental Release Measures

Evacuate the immediate area, isolate it, and eliminate ignition sources
because of the hydrogen hazard described in Section 2. Ventilate
enclosed spaces if this can be done without entering them.

Responders must wear acid-resistant suit, gloves, boots and full face
protection, with respiratory protection where mist may be present.

Contain the spill with dry inert material — dry sand, earth or a
proprietary acid absorbent. Do not flush the spill to drain, and do not
use water to move or dilute a bulk spill.

Neutralisation of a contained spill with soda ash, lime or sodium
bicarbonate may be carried out by trained personnel, cautiously, from
the edge inward, adding the neutraliser slowly to the acid and never
the reverse. The reaction foams vigorously and releases carbon dioxide
and heat, and adding neutraliser quickly to a large volume produces a
boiling, spattering mass of acid. On a large spill, containment and
professional removal is preferable to neutralisation.

Collect neutralised residue for disposal as chemical waste. Wash the
area only after the bulk acid has been absorbed or neutralised, and
check the washings before allowing them to drain.

Section 7 — Handling and Storage

Always add acid to water, slowly, with stirring. Never add water to
concentrated acid. Water added to acid floats on the denser acid and
the heat of mixing is released in a thin layer at the surface, which
can reach boiling point locally and eject acid violently out of the
vessel. Acid added to water disperses the same heat through the whole
volume. This ordering is the single most important handling rule for
this substance and it is the one most often reversed under time
pressure.

Store in a cool, dry, well-ventilated area with a bunded, acid-
resistant floor that does not drain to a public sewer. Keep containers
closed and upright.

Segregate from water-reactive materials, from strong bases and other
alkalis, from metals, from chlorates, perchlorates, permanganates,
carbides and fulminates, and from all organic and combustible
materials. Segregate by distance or barrier, not by labelling alone.

Use acid-resistant transfer equipment and never pressurise a carboy to
empty it. Provide an emergency shower and eyewash immediately adjacent
to any point where acid is decanted, and verify by test that they
deliver a large and sustained flow.

Section 10 — Stability and Reactivity

Stable under the storage conditions described above. Hygroscopic;
absorbs water from the air.

Reacts violently and exothermically with water, particularly when water
is added to the acid rather than the reverse.

Attacks most common metals, including iron, steel, aluminium and zinc,
liberating hydrogen. Hydrogen is flammable from about 4 to 75 per cent
in air and ignites on very little energy, so an acid spill in contact
with structural steel or a metal bund in a poorly ventilated space
creates an explosion risk that is not obvious from the substance's own
non-flammability.

Reacts violently with strong bases, releasing large amounts of heat.

Reacts dangerously with chlorates, perchlorates, permanganates,
carbides, fulminates and many organic compounds, in several cases
igniting them. Contact with organic material chars and may ignite it.

Hazardous decomposition products include sulphur oxides and, on contact
with metals, hydrogen.
